title: Cap. III Rat. 6: mercy with justice needs elect congruitas; Javellus
latin: Rat. 6. In omnibus operibus Dei misericordia concurrit cum justitia: Ergo ponere debemus ex parte electi aliquam convenientiam sive congruitatem, quae non fuit ex parte reprobi; secus nullum justitiae vestigium in hac Dei electione apparebit: Et quod elegit ex praevisione, et non ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae. Est argumentum Javelli in Quaestionibus adjunctis primae parti Aquinatis.
pass_a: Reason 6. In all the works of God mercy concurs with justice: Therefore we ought to posit on the part of the elect some fittingness or congruity which was not on the part of the reprobate; otherwise no vestige of justice will appear in this election of God: And that he elects from foresight, and not from the mere good pleasure of his will. It is the argument of Javellus in the Questions annexed to the first part of Aquinas.
pass_b: Rat. 6. In all God's works mercy concurs with justice — so, they say, we must posit on the elect's side some fittingness or congruity that was not on the reprobate's; otherwise no trace of justice will show in this election of God — and that he elects from foresight, not from the mere good pleasure of his will. So argues Javellus in the Questions annexed to Aquinas's Prima Pars.

lemmas.gloss: mercy concurs with justice in all works
Javellus: elect from foresight not mere good pleasure

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 6: if justice means congruent merit, concurrence impossible
latin: Sol. Sed respondeo; Si justitiam aliam Javellus intelligat, praeter illam quae sita est in hoc, quod Deus agat prout convenit bonitati suae et fidelitati, nego justitiam reperiri in omnibus illis actionibus, in quibus miseris hominibus facit benigne. Cum igitur Javellus ita justitiam Dei intelligat, ut juste agere inde dicatur, quod in beneficio electionis respiciat ad aliquod meritum congruum hominis; hoc sensu, justitiam concurrere cum misericordia in omni actione erga homines, dico non solummodo esse, sed impossibile.
pass_a: Solution. But I answer; If Javellus understands another justice, besides that which is situated in this, that God acts as befits his goodness and faithfulness, I deny that justice is found in all those actions in which he deals kindly with wretched human beings. Since therefore Javellus so understands the justice of God, that he is said to act justly thence, that in the benefit of election he regards some congruent merit of the human being; in this sense, that justice concurs with mercy in every action toward human beings, I say it is not only not so, but impossible.
pass_b: Sol. I answer: if Javellus means some justice other than that God acts as befits his own goodness and faithfulness, I deny that justice is found in every act where he deals kindly with wretched people. And if he so takes God's justice that acting justly means, in the gift of election, looking to some congruent human merit — then, in that sense, justice concurring with mercy in every dealing with people is not only false but impossible.

lemmas.gloss: justice as acting fitting God's goodness

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 6: Aquinas — justice presupposes mercy; first gift free adoption
latin: Nam, ut optime Aquinas Part. I. qu. 21. art. 4, Omne opus Divinae justitiae semper praesupponit opus misericordiae, in quo fundatum sit. Nil igitur procedere velimus in infinitum, deveniamus necesse est ad aliquod primum, quod ex sola misericordia et bonitate Divinae voluntatis dependet. Hoc autem quid aliud esse potest, quam gratuita illa adoptio et destinatio electorum ad vitam aeternam?
pass_a: For, as Aquinas excellently says, Part I question 21 article 4, Every work of divine justice always presupposes a work of mercy, in which it is founded. Therefore lest we wish to proceed to infinity, we must come to some first thing, which depends on the mercy and goodness alone of the divine will. But what else can this be, than that gratuitous adoption and destination of the elect to eternal life?
pass_b: For as Aquinas puts it best (ST I q.21 a.4): every work of divine justice always presupposes a work of mercy on which it is founded. So we must not run to infinity — we have to arrive at some first thing that depends on the mercy and goodness of the divine will alone. And what else can that be than the gratuitous adoption and destination of the elect to eternal life?

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 6 close: no praevisa congruentia; Miserebor cujus misertus fuero
latin: Ad hoc igitur primum beneficium, ut appareat in eo ratio quaedam justitiae, non debemus requirere praevisam aliquam congruentiam in electis: sed eatenus hoc justum est, quatenus convenit voluntati et bonitati Divinae sic agere velle, juxta illud, Miserebor cujus misertus fuero; non autem, Miserebor illorum in quibus, ut hoc juste simul faciam, merita quaedam congrua praevidero.
pass_a: To this first benefit, therefore, that some reason of justice may appear in it, we ought not to require some foreseen congruity in the elect: but to that extent this is just, inasmuch as it befits the divine will and goodness to will so to act, according to that, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy; not however, I will have mercy on those in whom, that I may at the same time do this justly, I shall have foreseen certain congruent merits.
pass_b: So for this first benefit, if some reason of justice is to appear in it, we must not require a foreseen congruity in the elect. It is just insofar as it befits the divine will and goodness to will to act so — according to I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy — not I will have mercy on those in whom, that I may do this justly at once, I shall have foreseen certain congruent merits.

lemmas.gloss: not mercy from foreseen congruent merits
